prose_changes.old: Basil's own preaching indicted the region's grain-hoarders by name and built a hospital, hostel, and workhouse complex outside Caesarea after the famine of 368 — a genuine, near-unprecedented undertaking, though not, as later legend sometimes claims, the first of its kind anywhere.
prose_changes.new: Basil's own preaching indicted the region's grain-hoarders and moved them to open their stores. After the famine of 368 he built a hospital, hostel, and workhouse complex outside Caesarea. It was a genuine, near-unprecedented undertaking, though not, as later legend sometimes claims, the first of its kind anywhere.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored text has Basil name the hoarders. Gregory of Nazianzus (Or. 43, NPNF 2.7) says he 'opened the stores of those who possessed them' by his word; Jackson's prolegomena (NPNF 2.8) say the same. The sentence also made 'preaching' the subject of 'built'.

prose_changes.old: The years were not peaceful throughout: this Christian tradition buried its own martyr, Eupsychius of Caesarea, executed under Julian in 362, and endured a hostile imperial church under Valens that drove Gregory of Nyssa briefly into exile.
prose_changes.new: The years were not peaceful throughout. This Christian tradition buried its own martyr, Eupsychius of Caesarea, executed under Julian in 362. Under Valens, a hostile church party had Gregory of Nyssa deposed, and he lived in exile until 378.
prose_changes.reason: 'Briefly' is not what the sources show and clashes with the entry's own voices text ('exiled under Valens for years'): Basil's letters date the deposition to about 376, and the NPNF 7 headnote dates his return to Valens's death in 378.

prose_changes.old: Damasus's own secretary was Jerome, who carried Rome's claims into the next generation's ascetic-literary circles; the Nicene settlement received at Chalcedon in 451 is the same creed the Cappadocian churches had helped work out a generation earlier.
prose_changes.new: Jerome served as secretary to Damasus of Rome. He had earlier written to Damasus that he kept communion only with 'the chair of Peter'. The creed received at Chalcedon in 451 came from the council of 381, where bishops of the Cappadocian churches took part.
prose_changes.reason: Jerome's letters show the secretaryship and his loyalty to 'the chair of Peter' (Epp. 15, 123), not that he carried Rome's claims into later circles. No vendored text says the Cappadocians helped work out the creed of 381, and 381 is seventy years before Chalcedon, not 'a generation'. Socrates V.8 and CTh 16.1.3 show them at and favored by the council.

prose_changes.old: He would not give it up, and his congregation stayed inside with him — prepared, an eyewitness later wrote, to die with their bishop. It was there, waiting through the night, that Milan's people first sang hymns the way the Eastern churches did, a custom that, by that eyewitness's account, never stopped and spread to churches across the world.
prose_changes.new: He would not give it up, and his congregation stayed inside with him. Augustine, then living in Milan, later wrote that they were 'prepared to die with their bishop'. He also wrote that at this time Milan's people began to sing hymns and psalms in the Eastern way. That custom, he says, lasted and spread to almost all congregations elsewhere.
prose_changes.reason: Augustine was not inside the basilica. Confessions IX.7 says his mother kept watch there, while 'we ... were yet moved by the astonished and disturbed city'. He was a witness in the city, not an eyewitness of the siege, and he does not mention a night.

prose_changes.old: Waiting through the siege night in 386, Ambrose's besieged congregation began singing psalms 'after the manner of the Eastern Church' — and Augustine, who was there, says the custom was 'retained from then till now' and copied by 'almost all' congregations 'throughout the rest of the world.'
prose_changes.new: During the siege of 386, Ambrose's congregation began singing psalms 'after the manner of the Eastern Church'. Augustine, then living in Milan, says the custom was 'retained from then till now'. He adds that 'almost all' congregations 'throughout the rest of the world' copied it.
prose_changes.reason: Same correction as the longDescription: Confessions IX.7 places Augustine in the city, not in the basilica, and mentions no night. The four quoted phrases are unchanged and appear verbatim in the NPNF 1.1 text.

prose_changes.old: Historical-literal exegesis, set against Alexandria's allegorical method; Theodore of Mopsuestia's own contested status is noted here on the record.
prose_changes.new: Historical-literal exegesis, set against Alexandria's allegorical method, though scholars dispute how sharp the contrast was. Theodore of Mopsuestia wrote against Origen, was condemned in 553, and was defended by the Church of the East as its 'Interpreter'.
prose_changes.reason: 'Noted here on the record' is cataloguing language. The project's Antiochene world already tags the broad literal-versus-allegorical contrast Contested (aec_Superseded_Claims 3.3). Theodore's book against Origen (Facundus III.6), the 553 canon and the 585 synod's defense are all in vendored texts.

prose_changes.old: They were quarried for medieval preaching, printed early and often in the Reformation era — Reformed and Lutheran preachers alike claimed him as an ancestor of expository preaching.
prose_changes.new: Reformation writers quoted him too. Calvin prized his saying that humility is 'the foundation of our philosophy', though he thought Chrysostom gave the human will too much power. The Augsburg Confession of 1530 cited him on how the early church shared Communion.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored or repo-cited source shows medieval quarrying, early printing, or a Reformed or Lutheran claim of ancestry for expository preaching. Calvin's Institutes (II.2.4, II.2.11) and the Augsburg Confession (XXIV) show the use that is documented.

prose_changes.old: The Antiochene way of reading, insisting that a text means what it meant to those who first heard it, is the ancestor of the historical-grammatical method that later Western biblical scholarship made standard.
prose_changes.new: The Antiochene way of reading insisted that a text means what it meant to those who first heard it. Later Western biblical scholarship made a similar historical-grammatical method standard, though no direct line between the two has been traced.
prose_changes.reason: 'Is the ancestor of' is a genealogical claim no vendored or repo-cited source supports. The likeness of method is fair to state; the descent is not.

prose_changes.old: It worshipped in Syriac, thought in the exegetical idiom it shared with Edessa and Antioch, and was already becoming the church that would carry Christianity along the trade roads to India, Central Asia, and China.
prose_changes.new: It worshipped in Syriac and shared the learning of Edessa. Persian students there read Theodore of Mopsuestia's commentaries once they were put into Syriac, and the church's later teachers made his Antiochene way of reading their own. And it was already becoming the church that would carry Christianity along the trade roads to India, Central Asia, and China.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored text shows the Persian church before 451 sharing Antioch's exegetical idiom. Barhadbeshabba (Cause of the Schools) shows Persian students at Edessa studying Theodore in Syriac; the synod of 585 shows the later church adopting him.
